# Read all XML/EML files from Global_data and subfolders
```{r}
# ============================================================
# Extract site_id and geographic coordinates
# Separately for each data type
# ============================================================

library(xml2)
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)
library(tibble)


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Main folder
# ------------------------------------------------------------

main_folder <- "C:\\Users\\uqegirol\\OneDrive - The University of Queensland\\Desktop\\Documents\\Accelnet project\\Data\\Global_data"


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Find all XML files
# ------------------------------------------------------------

xml_files <- list.files(
  path = main_folder,
  pattern = "\\.xml$",
  recursive = TRUE,
  full.names = TRUE,
  ignore.case = TRUE
)

cat("Number of XML files found:", length(xml_files), "\n")


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Function to extract information from one XML file
# ------------------------------------------------------------

extract_site_info <- function(xml_file) {
  
  # Read XML
  x <- tryCatch(
    read_xml(xml_file),
    error = function(e) {
      warning("Could not read: ", xml_file)
      return(NULL)
    }
  )
  
  if (is.null(x)) {
    return(NULL)
  }
  
  # Data type = folder containing XML
  data_type <- basename(dirname(xml_file))
  
  
  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # Find ALL site contexts
  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  
  sitecontexts <- xml_find_all(
    x,
    ".//*[local-name()='sitecontext']"
  )
  
  
  # If no sitecontexts are found
  if (length(sitecontexts) == 0) {
    return(NULL)
  }
  
  
  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # Extract information from each site
  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  
  map_dfr(seq_along(sitecontexts), function(i) {
    
    sitecontext <- sitecontexts[[i]]
    
    
    # --------------------------------------------------------
    # Site ID
    # --------------------------------------------------------
    
    site_id_node <- xml_find_first(
      sitecontext,
      ".//*[local-name()='site_id']"
    )
    
    site_id <- if (!inherits(site_id_node, "xml_missing")) {
      xml_text(site_id_node)
    } else {
      NA_character_
    }
    
    # --------------------------------------------------------
    # Site name
    # --------------------------------------------------------
    
    site_name_node <- xml_find_first(
      sitecontext,
      ".//*[local-name()='site_name']"
    )
    
    site_name <- if (!inherits(site_name_node, "xml_missing")) {
      xml_text(site_name_node)
    } else {
      NA_character_
    }


    # --------------------------------------------------------
    # Geographic coverage
    # --------------------------------------------------------
    
    geographic_coverages <- xml_find_all(
      x,
      ".//*[local-name()='geographicCoverage']"
    )
    
    
    # Use the geographic coverage corresponding to this site
    if (i <= length(geographic_coverages)) {
      
      geographic_coverage <- geographic_coverages[[i]]
      
      west_node <- xml_find_first(
        geographic_coverage,
        ".//*[local-name()='westBoundingCoordinate']"
      )
      
      east_node <- xml_find_first(
        geographic_coverage,
        ".//*[local-name()='eastBoundingCoordinate']"
      )
      
      north_node <- xml_find_first(
        geographic_coverage,
        ".//*[local-name()='northBoundingCoordinate']"
      )
      
      south_node <- xml_find_first(
        geographic_coverage,
        ".//*[local-name()='southBoundingCoordinate']"
      )
      
      west <- if (!inherits(west_node, "xml_missing")) {
        suppressWarnings(as.numeric(xml_text(west_node)))
      } else {
        NA_real_
      }
      
      east <- if (!inherits(east_node, "xml_missing")) {
        suppressWarnings(as.numeric(xml_text(east_node)))
      } else {
        NA_real_
      }
      
      north <- if (!inherits(north_node, "xml_missing")) {
        suppressWarnings(as.numeric(xml_text(north_node)))
      } else {
        NA_real_
      }
      
      south <- if (!inherits(south_node, "xml_missing")) {
        suppressWarnings(as.numeric(xml_text(south_node)))
      } else {
        NA_real_
      }
      
      longitude <- mean(c(west, east), na.rm = TRUE)
      latitude <- mean(c(south, north), na.rm = TRUE)
      
      if (is.nan(longitude)) longitude <- NA_real_
      if (is.nan(latitude)) latitude <- NA_real_
      
    } else {
      
      latitude <- NA_real_
      longitude <- NA_real_
      
    }
    
    
    # --------------------------------------------------------
    # Return one row for this site
    # --------------------------------------------------------
    
    tibble(
      data_type = data_type,
      site_id = site_id,
      site_name = site_name,
      latitude = latitude,
      longitude = longitude,
      file = xml_file
    )
  })
}

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Extract all XML files
# ------------------------------------------------------------

all_site_data <- map_dfr(
  xml_files,
  extract_site_info
)


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Remove records without a site ID
# ------------------------------------------------------------

all_site_data <- all_site_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(site_id))


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. Create one table per data type
# ------------------------------------------------------------

air_temperature <- all_site_data %>%
  filter(data_type == "Air_temperature") %>%
  distinct(site_id, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  select(site_id, site_name, latitude, longitude)

precipitation <- all_site_data %>%
  filter(data_type == "Precipitation") %>%
  distinct(site_id, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  select(site_id, site_name, latitude, longitude)

soil_moisture <- all_site_data %>%
  filter(data_type == "Soil_moisture") %>%
  distinct(site_id, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  select(site_id, site_name,latitude, longitude)

soil_temperature <- all_site_data %>%
  filter(data_type == "Soil_temperature") %>%
  distinct(site_id, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  select(site_id, site_name, latitude, longitude)

soil_texture <- all_site_data %>%
  filter(data_type == "Soil_texture") %>%
  distinct(site_id, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  select(site_id, site_name, latitude, longitude)

```


# Temporal coverage 
```{r}
# Temporal coverage - Air temperature
library(ggplot2)
library(lubridate)
library(dplyr)

# convert the two date columns to proper date-time values
GERI_airtemperature_30min <- GERI_airtemperature_30min %>%
  mutate(
    start_date_time = as.POSIXct(start_date_time),
    end_date_time = as.POSIXct(end_date_time)
  )

# determine the gaps in the air-temperature data
airtemperature_gaps <- GERI_airtemperature_30min %>%
  arrange(site_id, start_date_time) %>%
  group_by(site_id, site_name) %>%
  mutate(
    gap = start_date_time - lag(end_date_time)
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(gap) & gap > 30 * 60)

# turn the data into continuous coverage periods. Each period will become one horizontal segment in the graph, so gaps will be visible.
airtemperature_periods <- GERI_airtemperature_30min %>%
  filter(!is.na(mean_air_temp_degC)) %>%
  arrange(site_id, start_date_time) %>%
  group_by(site_id, site_name) %>%
  mutate(
    gap = start_date_time - lag(end_date_time),
    period = cumsum(
      is.na(gap) | gap > 30 * 60
    )
  ) %>%
  group_by(site_id, site_name, period) %>%
  summarise(
    start_date = min(start_date_time, na.rm = TRUE),
    end_date = max(end_date_time, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )


```


# create the temporal coverage graph
```{r air-temperature-coverage, fig.width=12, fig.height=15}
ggplot(
  airtemperature_periods,
  aes(
    x = start_date,
    xend = end_date,
    y = site_id,
    yend = site_id
  )
) +
  geom_segment(linewidth = 3) +
  labs(
    title = "Air temperature temporal coverage",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Site"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```

```{r}


## 3. Where are the monitoring sites located?

#Mapping environmental monitoring sites allows us to visualise their geographic distribution and identify regions where observations may be limited.

#We will first create a combined global map showing all environmental variables, followed by separate maps for each variable. This will help us identify overlapping monitoring sites and compare geographic coverage.


# Load the package containing world map boundaries
library(maps)

# Prepare the site coordinates for mapping
# Keep one record per site for each environmental variable
site_map_data <- all_site_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(latitude), !is.na(longitude)) %>%
  distinct(data_type, site_id, .keep_all = TRUE)

# Load world map boundaries
world <- ggplot2::map_data("world")


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Combined map showing all environmental variables
# ------------------------------------------------------------

combined_map <- ggplot() +
  geom_polygon(
    data = world,
    aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group),
    fill = "grey90",
    colour = "white"
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = site_map_data,
    aes(x = longitude, y = latitude, colour = data_type),
    size = 2,
    alpha = 0.7
  ) +
  coord_quickmap() +
  labs(
    title = "Global distribution of environmental monitoring sites",
    x = "Longitude",
    y = "Latitude",
    colour = "Environmental variable"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# Display the combined map
print(combined_map)


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Separate maps for each environmental variable
# ------------------------------------------------------------

separate_maps <- ggplot() +
  geom_polygon(
    data = world,
    aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group),
    fill = "grey90",
    colour = "white"
  ) +
  
geom_point(
  data = site_map_data,
  aes(x = longitude, y = latitude, colour = data_type),
  size = 2,
  alpha = 0.7
) +

  coord_quickmap() +
  facet_wrap(~ data_type, ncol = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "Geographic coverage by environmental variable",
    x = "Longitude",
    y = "Latitude"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# Display the five separate maps
print(separate_maps)
```

```{r}

# Check whether the environmental variables share the same sites
# This helps us determine whether the similar maps are expected.

# Create a list of site IDs for each environmental variable
site_lists <- split(
  site_map_data$site_id,
  site_map_data$data_type
)

# Compare the site IDs between environmental variables
# TRUE means both variables have exactly the same site IDs
# FALSE means their site lists differ

site_comparison <- outer(
  names(site_lists),
  names(site_lists),
  Vectorize(function(x, y) {
    setequal(site_lists[[x]], site_lists[[y]])
  })
)

# Add variable names to the comparison table
dimnames(site_comparison) <- list(
  names(site_lists),
  names(site_lists)
)

# Display the results
print(site_comparison)

```

```{r}
# Check the earliest and latest observations in each dataset


# Summarise the environmental datasets
# Show observations, sites, research infrastructures and date ranges

library(dplyr)

data_summary <- bind_rows(
  lapply(names(parquet_data), function(file) {

    x <- parquet_data[[file]]

    # Static soil texture data use date_collected
    # Other datasets use start_date_time and end_date_time
    if ("start_date_time" %in% names(x)) {
      first_date <- min(as.Date(x$start_date_time), na.rm = TRUE)
      last_date <- max(as.Date(x$end_date_time), na.rm = TRUE)
    } else {
      first_date <- min(as.Date(x$date_collected), na.rm = TRUE)
      last_date <- max(as.Date(x$date_collected), na.rm = TRUE)
    }

    data.frame(
      dataset = tools::file_path_sans_ext(file),
      observations = nrow(x),
      sites = n_distinct(x$site_id),
      research_infrastructures = n_distinct(x$research_infrastructure),
      first_date = first_date,
      last_date = last_date
    )
  })
)

# Display all five datasets in one table
print(data_summary)

```

```{r}

# Summarise temporal coverage for all four environmental variables
# Soil texture is excluded because it is not a time-series dataset

# Identify the four time-series datasets
time_series_files <- c(
  "GERI_airtemperature_30min.parquet",
  "GERI_precipitation_60min.parquet",
  "GERI_soilmoisture_30min.parquet",
  "GERI_soiltemperature_30min.parquet"
)

# Give the variables readable names
variable_names <- c(
  "Air temperature",
  "Precipitation",
  "Soil moisture",
  "Soil temperature"
)

# Combine the summaries into one table
coverage_summary <- bind_rows(
  lapply(seq_along(time_series_files), function(i) {

    parquet_data[[time_series_files[i]]] %>%
      group_by(research_infrastructure) %>%
      summarise(
        n_sites = n_distinct(site_id),
        first_date = as.Date(min(start_date_time, na.rm = TRUE)),
        last_date = as.Date(max(end_date_time, na.rm = TRUE)),
        .groups = "drop"
      ) %>%
      mutate(variable = variable_names[i], .before = 1)

  })
)

# Display the combined table
print(coverage_summary, n = Inf)

```

```{r}
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. How does temporal coverage differ between environmental variables?
# ------------------------------------------------------------

# Environmental datasets may differ in the periods over which
# observations have been collected.
#
# Comparing temporal coverage helps us identify which datasets
# may be suitable for investigating long-term environmental
# changes, including drought.
#
# This graph shows the earliest and latest observations for
# each research infrastructure, separately for four variables.
#
# Note: Lines show the overall date range, not continuous
# monitoring throughout that period.


# Create a temporal coverage graph
ggplot(
  coverage_summary,
  aes(
    x = first_date,
    xend = last_date,
    y = research_infrastructure,
    yend = research_infrastructure,
    colour = research_infrastructure
  )
) +
  geom_segment(linewidth = 3) +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, ncol = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "Temporal coverage of environmental observations",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Research infrastructure",
    colour = "Research infrastructure"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +

  )
```

# Australia
# Maps of Australian sites (one map for each variable)
# Plot time series (one for each long-term variable) > tell cool stories about local events, e.g. soil temp at Robson


```{r}
# Select only sites with AU- in the site_id
# Convert date-time and identify gaps in the 30-minute time series
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggforce)
GERI_soilmoisture_30min_AU <- GERI_soilmoisture_30min %>%
  filter(grepl("AU-", site_id)) %>%
  mutate(
    start_date_time = as.POSIXct(start_date_time)
  ) %>%
  arrange(site_id, start_date_time) %>%
  group_by(site_id) %>%
  mutate(
    time_gap = as.numeric(
      difftime(
        start_date_time,
        lag(start_date_time),
        units = "mins"
      )
    ),
    # Start a new line segment when there is a gap
    # of more than 31 minutes
    segment = cumsum(
      if_else(
        is.na(time_gap) | time_gap > 31,
        1,
        0
      )
    )
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

# Number of sites
n_sites <- n_distinct(GERI_soilmoisture_30min_AU$site_id)

# Number of pages needed (9 sites per page)
n_pages <- ceiling(n_sites / 9)

cat("Number of AU sites:", n_sites, "\n")
cat("Number of pages:", n_pages, "\n")

# Create one plot per page
for (page in 1:n_pages) {
  
  p <- ggplot(
    GERI_soilmoisture_30min_AU,
    aes(
      x = start_date_time,
      y = mean_swc_percent
    )
  ) +
    geom_line(
      aes(group = interaction(site_id, segment))
    ) +
    facet_wrap_paginate(
      ~ site_id,
      ncol = 3,
      nrow = 3,
      page = page,
      scales = "free_x"
    ) +
    labs(
      x = "Date",
      y = "Mean soil moisture (percent)",
      title = paste(
        "Soil moisture time series — AU sites",
        "(page", page, "of", n_pages, ")"
      )
    ) +
    theme_bw()
  
  print(p)
}
```

```{r}
    start_date_time = as.POSIXct(start_date_time)
  ) %>%
  arrange(site_id, start_date_time) %>%
  group_by(site_id) %>%
  mutate(
    time_gap = as.numeric(
      difftime(
        start_date_time,
        lag(start_date_time),
        units = "mins"
      )
    ),
    # Start a new line segment when there is a gap
    # of more than 31 minutes
    segment = cumsum(
      if_else(
        is.na(time_gap) | time_gap > 61,
        1,
        0
      )
    )
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

# Number of sites
n_sites <- n_distinct(GERI_airtemperature_30min_AU$site_id)

# Number of pages needed (9 sites per page)
n_pages <- ceiling(n_sites / 9)

cat("Number of AU sites:", n_sites, "\n")
cat("Number of pages:", n_pages, "\n")

# Create one plot per page
for (page in 1:n_pages) {
  
  p <- ggplot(
    GERI_airtemperature_30min_AU,
    aes(
      x = start_date_time,
      y = mean_air_temp_degC
    )
  ) +
    geom_line(
      aes(group = interaction(site_id, segment))
    ) +
    facet_wrap_paginate(
      ~ site_id,
      ncol = 3,
      nrow = 3,
      page = page,
      scales = "free_x"
    ) +
    labs(
      x = "Date",
      y = "Mean air temperature (degrees)",
      title = paste(
        "Air temperature time series — AU sites",
        "(page", page, "of", n_pages, ")"
      )
    ) +
    theme_bw()
  
  print(p)
}

```

```{r}

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Robson Creek: monthly soil temperature and soil moisture
# ------------------------------------------------------------

# Scientific investigation
#
# Did soil temperature increase at the same time that
# soil moisture decreased?
#
# When did these changes begin?
#
# Are the changes consistent with normal seasonal patterns,
# or do they represent a shift in local soil conditions?
#
# Did soil temperatures increase because the surrounding air
# became hotter, or because conditions at the soil surface changed?
#
# If soil temperature rises dramatically while air temperature
# maintains its previous seasonal pattern, that would strengthen
# the case for a local canopy effect.
#
# Examine the period 2023–2026 to investigate the recent changes.

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)
library(lubridate)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Calculate monthly mean soil temperature
# ------------------------------------------------------------

robson_soiltemperature_monthly <- robson_soiltemperature_daily %>%
  mutate(month = floor_date(date, unit = "month")) %>%
  group_by(month) %>%
  summarise(
    soil_temperature = mean(
      mean_soil_temperature,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Calculate monthly mean soil moisture
# ------------------------------------------------------------

robson_soilmoisture_monthly <- robson_soilmoisture_daily %>%
  mutate(month = floor_date(date, unit = "month")) %>%
  group_by(month) %>%
  summarise(
    soil_moisture = mean(
      mean_soil_moisture,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Combine the two monthly datasets
# ------------------------------------------------------------

robson_monthly_soil <- full_join(
  robson_soiltemperature_monthly,
  robson_soilmoisture_monthly,
  by = "month"
) %>%
  filter(
    month >= as.Date("2023-01-01"),
    month <= as.Date("2026-12-31")
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(soil_temperature, soil_moisture),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "value"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    variable = recode(
      variable,
      soil_temperature = "Soil temperature (°C)",
      soil_moisture = "Soil moisture (%)"
    )
  )

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Plot the monthly averages
# ------------------------------------------------------------

ggplot(
  robson_monthly_soil,
  aes(x = month, y = value)
) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~ variable,
    ncol = 1,
    scales = "free_y"
  ) +
  scale_x_date(
    date_breaks = "3 months",
    date_labels = "%b %Y"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Robson Creek: monthly soil temperature and moisture",
    subtitle = "January 2023–2026",
    x = "Month",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(
      angle = 45,
      hjust = 1
    )
  )

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Interpretation
# ------------------------------------------------------------

# Identify the month when soil temperature begins to rise
# beyond its earlier seasonal pattern.
#
# Does soil moisture decline during the same months?
#
# Is there a delay between the two changes?
#
# Could both patterns be explained by seasonal variation?
#
# Would comparing the same months in earlier years help
# distinguish seasonal effects from a possible canopy effect?
#
# IMPORTANT:
# These observations do not establish that tree removal
# caused the changes. The event date, rainfall patterns,
# sensor history and other environmental factors should
# also be investigated.

```

```{r}
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Robson Creek: monthly soil temperature, soil moisture
# and precipitation
# ------------------------------------------------------------

# Scientific investigation
#
# Did soil temperatures increase because the surrounding air
# became hotter, or because conditions at the soil surface changed?
#
# If soil temperature rises dramatically while air temperature
# maintains its previous seasonal pattern, that would strengthen
# the case for a local canopy effect.
#
# Did soil moisture decline when soil temperature increased?
#
# Was the decline in soil moisture associated with reduced rainfall?
#
# If rainfall remained relatively consistent, could changes
# in canopy cover or local soil conditions help explain the results?
#
# Examine the timing of changes across all three variables.

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)
library(lubridate)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Calculate monthly mean soil temperature
# ------------------------------------------------------------

robson_soiltemperature_monthly <- robson_soiltemperature_daily %>%
  mutate(month = floor_date(date, unit = "month")) %>%
  group_by(month) %>%
  summarise(
    soil_temperature = mean(
      mean_soil_temperature,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Calculate monthly mean soil moisture
# ------------------------------------------------------------

robson_soilmoisture_monthly <- robson_soilmoisture_daily %>%
  mutate(month = floor_date(date, unit = "month")) %>%
  group_by(month) %>%
  summarise(
    soil_moisture = mean(
      mean_soil_moisture,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Calculate monthly total precipitation
# ------------------------------------------------------------

# Sum daily precipitation totals to obtain monthly rainfall.
# Count days with observations to help assess data completeness.

robson_precipitation_monthly <- robson_precipitation_daily %>%
  mutate(month = floor_date(date, unit = "month")) %>%
  group_by(month) %>%
  summarise(
    precipitation = sum(daily_precipitation, na.rm = TRUE),
    days_with_data = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Combine the three monthly datasets
# ------------------------------------------------------------

robson_monthly_environment <- robson_soiltemperature_monthly %>%
  full_join(
    robson_soilmoisture_monthly,
    by = "month"
  ) %>%
  full_join(
    robson_precipitation_monthly,
    by = "month"
  ) %>%
  filter(
    month >= as.Date("2023-01-01"),
    month <= as.Date("2026-12-31")
  ) %>%
  select(month, soil_temperature, soil_moisture, precipitation) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(soil_temperature, soil_moisture, precipitation),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "value"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    variable = factor(
      variable,
      levels = c(
        "soil_moisture",
        "soil_temperature",
        "precipitation"
      ),
      labels = c(
        "Soil moisture (%)",
        "Soil temperature (°C)",
        "Monthly precipitation (mm)"
      )
    )
  )

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Plot all three variables
# ------------------------------------------------------------

ggplot(
  robson_monthly_environment,
  aes(x = month, y = value)
) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~ variable,
    ncol = 1,
    scales = "free_y"
  ) +
  scale_x_date(
    date_breaks = "3 months",
    date_labels = "%b %Y"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Robson Creek: monthly environmental conditions",
    subtitle = "Soil moisture, soil temperature and precipitation (2023–2026)",
    x = "Month",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(
      angle = 45,
      hjust = 1
    )
  )

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Interpretation
# ------------------------------------------------------------

# 1. When does soil temperature begin to increase?
#
# 2. Does soil moisture decline during the same period?
#
# 3. Does precipitation also decline, or does rainfall
#    remain relatively consistent?
#
# 4. Could reduced rainfall explain the soil moisture decline?
#
# 5. If rainfall does not decline, what other mechanisms
#    could explain the changes in soil temperature and moisture?
#
# 6. Is the timing consistent with the reported tree removal?
#
# IMPORTANT:
# Monthly rainfall totals may be underestimated where
# observations are missing. Check days_with_data before
# interpreting unusually low monthly rainfall.
#
# Correlation between variables does not establish causation.

```

```{r}
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Robson Creek: check hourly rainfall observations
# September to November 2025
# ------------------------------------------------------------

# Scientific investigation
#
# Were the zero monthly rainfall totals genuine?
#
# Did the precipitation sensor continue reporting observations?
#
# Were measurements missing, or were all recorded values zero?
#
# This check helps distinguish possible drought conditions
# from potential sensor or data-quality problems.

GERI_precipitation_60min %>%
  filter(
    site_id == "AU-Rob",
    as.Date(start_date_time) >= as.Date("2025-09-01"),
    as.Date(start_date_time) <= as.Date("2025-11-30")
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    month = format(as.Date(start_date_time), "%Y-%m")
  ) %>%
  group_by(month) %>%
  summarise(
    total_records = n(),
    valid_records = sum(!is.na(bulk_precipitation_mm)),
    missing_records = sum(is.na(bulk_precipitation_mm)),
    positive_rainfall_records = sum(
      bulk_precipitation_mm > 0,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    maximum_hourly_rainfall = if (
      all(is.na(bulk_precipitation_mm))
    ) NA_real_ else max(
      bulk_precipitation_mm,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

```{r}

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Robson Creek: monthly soil temperature anomalies
# ------------------------------------------------------------

# Scientific investigation
#
# Did soil temperatures increase because the surrounding air
# became hotter, or because conditions at the soil surface changed?
#
# If soil temperature rises dramatically while air temperature
# maintains its previous seasonal pattern, that would strengthen
# the case for a local canopy effect.
#
# An anomaly is the difference between an observed temperature
# and the historical average for the same calendar month.


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# What is a soil temperature anomaly?
# ------------------------------------------------------------

# A temperature anomaly measures how much an observed temperature
# differs from the historical average for the same time of year.
#
# For Robson Creek, we use 2013–2023 as the reference period.
#
# Step 1: Calculate the mean soil temperature for each month
#         in the Robson Creek dataset.
#
# Step 2: For each calendar month (January, February, etc.),
#         calculate the average of the monthly means across
#         the 2013–2023 reference period.
#
# Step 3: Subtract the historical average for that calendar
#         month from the observed monthly mean temperature.
#
# Soil temperature anomaly (°C) =
#   Observed monthly mean - Historical mean for the same month
#
# For example:
# If the historical October mean was 22°C and the observed
# October 2025 mean was 32°C, the anomaly would be +10°C.
#
# Positive anomalies indicate warmer-than-average conditions.
# Negative anomalies indicate cooler-than-average conditions.
#
# This approach accounts for normal seasonal temperature
# variation, making unusual changes easier to identify.
#
# The baseline is specific to Robson Creek and is not a
# standard 30-year climatological reference period.
#
# IMPORTANT:
# An anomaly identifies a departure from historical conditions.
# It does not establish what caused that departure.
# ------------------------------------------------------------

#
# Positive anomaly = warmer than the historical monthly average
# Negative anomaly = cooler than the historical monthly average
#
# Questions:
# 1. When do unusually warm soil temperatures begin?
# 2. How large are the recent anomalies?
# 3. Are the anomalies sustained across multiple months?
# 4. Is the pattern consistent with a local canopy change?
# 5. What other explanations should be considered?

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(lubridate)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Calculate monthly mean soil temperature
# ------------------------------------------------------------

robson_soiltemperature_monthly <- robson_soiltemperature_daily %>%
  mutate(
    month = floor_date(date, unit = "month")
  ) %>%
  group_by(month) %>%
  summarise(
    soil_temperature = mean(
      mean_soil_temperature,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Calculate the historical seasonal baseline
# ------------------------------------------------------------

# Use 2013–2023 as the provisional reference period
# Calculate the average for each calendar month

robson_soil_baseline <- robson_soiltemperature_monthly %>%
  mutate(
    year = year(month),
    calendar_month = month(month)
  ) %>%
  filter(
    year >= 2013,
    year <= 2023
  ) %>%
  group_by(calendar_month) %>%
  summarise(
    baseline_temperature = mean(
      soil_temperature,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Calculate monthly temperature anomalies
# ------------------------------------------------------------

robson_soil_anomalies <- robson_soiltemperature_monthly %>%
  mutate(
    calendar_month = month(month)
  ) %>%
  left_join(
    robson_soil_baseline,
    by = "calendar_month"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    temperature_anomaly =
      soil_temperature - baseline_temperature
  ) %>%
  filter(
    month >= as.Date("2023-01-01"),
    month <= as.Date("2026-12-31")
  )

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Plot monthly soil temperature anomalies
# ------------------------------------------------------------

ggplot(
  robson_soil_anomalies,
  aes(
    x = month,
    y = temperature_anomaly
  )
) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  geom_col(
    aes(fill = temperature_anomaly > 0),
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "TRUE" = "firebrick",
      "FALSE" = "steelblue"
    )
  ) +
  scale_x_date(
    date_breaks = "3 months",
    date_labels = "%b %Y"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Robson Creek: monthly soil temperature anomalies",
    subtitle = "Relative to the 2013–2023 seasonal baseline",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Soil temperature anomaly (°C)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(
      angle = 45,
      hjust = 1
    )
  )

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Interpretation
# ------------------------------------------------------------

# Are recent soil temperatures consistently above the
# historical seasonal average?
#
# Does the anomaly begin abruptly or increase gradually?
#
# How does the magnitude of the anomaly compare with
# earlier years?
#
# Could tree removal explain the change in soil microclimate?
#
# IMPORTANT:
# The anomaly does not establish causation.
# Confirm the tree-removal date and investigate sensor history
# before attributing the change to canopy removal.

```
```{r}

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Robson Creek: monthly soil moisture anomalies
# ------------------------------------------------------------

# Scientific investigation
#
# Did soil moisture decline at the same time that soil
# temperature increased?
#
# Is the recent decline in soil moisture unusual compared
# with historical conditions for the same time of year?
#
# Could changes in rainfall, evaporation, vegetation water
# uptake or canopy cover help explain the observed pattern?


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# What is a soil moisture anomaly?
# ------------------------------------------------------------

# A soil moisture anomaly measures how much observed soil
# moisture differs from the historical average for the
# same calendar month.
#
# For Robson Creek, we use 2013–2023 as the reference period.
#
# Step 1: Calculate mean soil moisture for each month.
#
# Step 2: For each calendar month (January, February, etc.),
#         calculate the average of monthly means across
#         the 2013–2023 reference period.
#
# Step 3: Subtract the historical average for that calendar
#         month from the observed monthly mean soil moisture.
#
# Soil moisture anomaly (percentage points) =
#   Observed monthly mean - Historical mean for the same month
#
# Example:
# If the historical October mean was 30% and the observed
# October 2025 mean was 20%, the anomaly would be -10
# percentage points.
#
# Positive anomalies indicate wetter-than-average soil.
# Negative anomalies indicate drier-than-average soil.
#
# This is a site-specific historical baseline, not a
# standard 30-year climatological reference period.
#
# IMPORTANT:
# An anomaly identifies a departure from historical conditions.
# It does not establish what caused that departure.


library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(lubridate)


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Calculate monthly mean soil moisture
# ------------------------------------------------------------

robson_soilmoisture_monthly <- robson_soilmoisture_daily %>%
  mutate(
    month = floor_date(date, unit = "month")
  ) %>%
  group_by(month) %>%
  summarise(
    soil_moisture = mean(
      mean_soil_moisture,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Calculate the historical seasonal baseline
# ------------------------------------------------------------

robson_moisture_baseline <- robson_soilmoisture_monthly %>%
  mutate(
    year = year(month),
    calendar_month = month(month)
  ) %>%
  filter(
    year >= 2013,
    year <= 2023
  ) %>%
  group_by(calendar_month) %>%
  summarise(
    baseline_moisture = mean(
      soil_moisture,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Calculate monthly soil moisture anomalies
# ------------------------------------------------------------

robson_moisture_anomalies <- robson_soilmoisture_monthly %>%
  mutate(
    calendar_month = month(month)
  ) %>%
  left_join(
    robson_moisture_baseline,
    by = "calendar_month"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    moisture_anomaly = soil_moisture - baseline_moisture
  ) %>%
  filter(
    month >= as.Date("2023-01-01"),
    month <= as.Date("2026-12-31")
  )


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Plot monthly soil moisture anomalies
# ------------------------------------------------------------

ggplot(
  robson_moisture_anomalies,
  aes(
    x = month,
    y = moisture_anomaly
  )
) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  geom_col(
    aes(fill = moisture_anomaly > 0),
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "TRUE" = "steelblue",
      "FALSE" = "firebrick"
    )
  ) +
  scale_x_date(
    date_breaks = "3 months",
    date_labels = "%b %Y"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Robson Creek: monthly soil moisture anomalies",
    subtitle = "Relative to the 2013–2023 seasonal baseline",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Soil moisture anomaly (percentage points)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(
      angle = 45,
      hjust = 1
    )
  )


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Interpretation
# ------------------------------------------------------------

# 1. Are soil moisture anomalies consistently negative
#    during the period of increasing soil temperature?
#
# 2. When do negative anomalies first appear?
#
# 3. Are the recent negative anomalies more extreme
#    than those observed in earlier years?
#
# 4. Could rainfall variation explain the soil moisture
#    anomalies, or might local soil conditions contribute?
#
# 5. Do the timing and magnitude of changes support
#    investigating the reported tree-removal event?
#
# Remember:
# Correlation does not establish causation.

```
```{r}

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Robson Creek: monthly precipitation anomalies
# ------------------------------------------------------------

# Scientific investigation
#
# Did rainfall decline during the period when soil
# temperature increased and soil moisture decreased?
#
# Were recent rainfall totals unusually low compared
# with historical conditions for the same time of year?
#
# Could reduced rainfall explain the negative soil
# moisture anomalies observed during 2025?
#
# Does the timing of rainfall anomalies correspond with
# the increase in soil temperature?


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# What is a precipitation anomaly?
# ------------------------------------------------------------

# A precipitation anomaly measures how much rainfall in a
# particular month differs from the historical average
# rainfall for that same calendar month.
#
# For Robson Creek, we use 2013–2023 as the reference period.
#
# Step 1: Sum daily rainfall to calculate the total
#         precipitation recorded in each month.
#
# Step 2: For each calendar month (January, February, etc.),
#         calculate the average monthly rainfall total
#         across the 2013–2023 reference period.
#
# Step 3: Subtract the historical average from the observed
#         monthly rainfall total.
#
# Precipitation anomaly (mm) =
#   Observed monthly total - Historical mean monthly total
#
# Example:
# If the historical October average was 150 mm and
# October 2025 recorded 50 mm, the anomaly would be -100 mm.
#
# Positive anomalies indicate wetter-than-average months.
# Negative anomalies indicate drier-than-average months.
#
# IMPORTANT DATA QUALITY NOTE:
#
# September, October and November 2025 contain zero
# recorded precipitation despite hourly observations.
#
# These values may reflect equipment failure or another
# data-quality issue. This has not yet been confirmed.
#
# The anomalies for these months must therefore be
# treated as provisional and should not be interpreted
# as evidence of drought until verified with the PI.


library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(lubridate)


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Calculate monthly precipitation totals
# ------------------------------------------------------------

robson_precipitation_monthly <- robson_precipitation_daily %>%
  mutate(
    month = floor_date(date, unit = "month")
  ) %>%
  group_by(month) %>%
  summarise(
    precipitation = sum(
      daily_precipitation,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    days_with_data = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Calculate the historical seasonal baseline
# ------------------------------------------------------------

robson_precipitation_baseline <- robson_precipitation_monthly %>%
  mutate(
    year = year(month),
    calendar_month = month(month)
  ) %>%
  filter(
    year >= 2013,
    year <= 2023
  ) %>%
  group_by(calendar_month) %>%
  summarise(
    baseline_precipitation = mean(
      precipitation,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Calculate monthly precipitation anomalies
# ------------------------------------------------------------

robson_precipitation_anomalies <- robson_precipitation_monthly %>%
  mutate(
    calendar_month = month(month)
  ) %>%
  left_join(
    robson_precipitation_baseline,
    by = "calendar_month"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    precipitation_anomaly =
      precipitation - baseline_precipitation
  ) %>%
  filter(
    month >= as.Date("2023-01-01"),
    month <= as.Date("2026-12-31")
  )


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Plot monthly precipitation anomalies
# ------------------------------------------------------------

ggplot(
  robson_precipitation_anomalies,
  aes(
    x = month,
    y = precipitation_anomaly
  )
) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  geom_col(
    aes(fill = precipitation_anomaly > 0),
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "TRUE" = "steelblue",
      "FALSE" = "firebrick"
    )
  ) +
  scale_x_date(
    date_breaks = "3 months",
    date_labels = "%b %Y"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Robson Creek: monthly precipitation anomalies",
    subtitle = "Relative to the 2013–2023 seasonal baseline; late 2025 data unverified",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Precipitation anomaly (mm)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(
      angle = 45,
      hjust = 1
    )
  )


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Interpretation
# ------------------------------------------------------------

# 1. Were precipitation anomalies predominantly negative
#    during the period of increasing soil temperature?
#
# 2. Do negative precipitation anomalies coincide with
#    negative soil moisture anomalies?
#
# 3. Were there unusually wet months immediately before
#    the apparent decline in rainfall?
#
# 4. Could rainfall variation explain some of the changes
#    in soil moisture and soil temperature?
#
# 5. How might equipment failure affect our interpretation
#    of precipitation anomalies?
#
# IMPORTANT:
# September–November 2025 precipitation data require
# confirmation from the PI before ecological interpretation.
#
# Monthly totals can also be underestimated when hourly
# measurements are missing, even if each day has some data.

```
```{r}

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Robson Creek: monthly air temperature anomalies
# ------------------------------------------------------------

# Scientific investigation
#
# Did soil temperatures increase because the surrounding air
# became hotter, or because conditions at the soil surface changed?
#
# If soil temperature rises dramatically while air temperature
# maintains its previous seasonal pattern, that would strengthen
# the case for a local canopy effect.
#
# Did air temperature increase during 2024–2025?
#
# Are recent air temperatures unusual compared with historical
# conditions for the same time of year?
#
# Do air temperature anomalies correspond with the pronounced
# positive soil temperature anomalies?


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# What is an air temperature anomaly?
# ------------------------------------------------------------

# An air temperature anomaly measures how much the observed
# monthly mean temperature differs from the historical
# average for the same calendar month.
#
# For Robson Creek, we use 2013–2023 as the reference period.
#
# Step 1: Calculate the mean air temperature for each month.
#
# Step 2: For each calendar month (January, February, etc.),
#         calculate the average of monthly means across
#         the 2013–2023 reference period.
#
# Step 3: Subtract the historical average for that calendar
#         month from the observed monthly mean temperature.
#
# Air temperature anomaly (°C) =
#   Observed monthly mean - Historical mean for the same month
#
# Example:
# If the historical October mean was 21°C and the observed
# October 2025 mean was 22°C, the anomaly would be +1°C.
#
# Positive anomalies indicate warmer-than-average conditions.
# Negative anomalies indicate cooler-than-average conditions.
#
# This is a site-specific historical baseline, not a
# standard 30-year climatological reference period.
#
# IMPORTANT:
# An anomaly identifies a departure from historical conditions.
# It does not establish what caused that departure.


library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(lubridate)


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Calculate daily mean air temperature
# ------------------------------------------------------------

robson_airtemperature_daily <- GERI_airtemperature_30min %>%
  filter(site_id == "AU-Rob") %>%
  mutate(
    start_date_time = as.POSIXct(start_date_time),
    date = as.Date(start_date_time)
  ) %>%
  group_by(date) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_air_temperature = mean(
      mean_air_temp_degC,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  filter(is.finite(mean_air_temperature))


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Calculate monthly mean air temperature
# ------------------------------------------------------------

robson_airtemperature_monthly <- robson_airtemperature_daily %>%
  mutate(
    month = floor_date(date, unit = "month")
  ) %>%
  group_by(month) %>%
  summarise(
    air_temperature = mean(
      mean_air_temperature,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Calculate the historical seasonal baseline
# ------------------------------------------------------------

robson_air_baseline <- robson_airtemperature_monthly %>%
  mutate(
    year = year(month),
    calendar_month = month(month)
  ) %>%
  filter(
    year >= 2013,
    year <= 2023
  ) %>%
  group_by(calendar_month) %>%
  summarise(
    baseline_temperature = mean(
      air_temperature,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Calculate monthly air temperature anomalies
# ------------------------------------------------------------

robson_air_anomalies <- robson_airtemperature_monthly %>%
  mutate(
    calendar_month = month(month)
  ) %>%
  left_join(
    robson_air_baseline,
    by = "calendar_month"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    temperature_anomaly =
      air_temperature - baseline_temperature
  ) %>%
  filter(
    month >= as.Date("2023-01-01"),
    month <= as.Date("2026-12-31")
  )


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Plot monthly air temperature anomalies
# ------------------------------------------------------------

ggplot(
  robson_air_anomalies,
  aes(
    x = month,
    y = temperature_anomaly
  )
) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  geom_col(
    aes(fill = temperature_anomaly > 0),
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "TRUE" = "firebrick",
      "FALSE" = "steelblue"
    )
  ) +
  scale_x_date(
    date_breaks = "3 months",
    date_labels = "%b %Y"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Robson Creek: monthly air temperature anomalies",
    subtitle = "Relative to the 2013–2023 seasonal baseline",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Air temperature anomaly (°C)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(
      angle = 45,
      hjust = 1
    )
  )


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Interpretation
# ------------------------------------------------------------

# 1. Are air temperature anomalies consistently positive
#    during 2024–2025?
#
# 2. How large are the air temperature anomalies compared
#    with the soil temperature anomalies?
#
# 3. Does air temperature show a similar upward shift
#    to soil temperature?
#
# 4. If soil temperature anomalies are much larger than
#    air temperature anomalies, what local environmental
#    changes could explain the difference?
#
# 5. Could canopy removal, changes in soil exposure or
#    sensor conditions explain the observed soil warming?
#
# IMPORTANT:
# Confirm the timing of tree removal and any changes
# in instrumentation before drawing causal conclusions.

```
```{r}

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Robson Creek: soil versus air temperature anomalies
# ------------------------------------------------------------

# Scientific investigation
#
# Did soil temperatures increase because the surrounding air
# became hotter, or because conditions at the soil surface changed?
#
# If soil temperature rises dramatically while air temperature
# maintains its previous seasonal pattern, that would strengthen
# the case for a local canopy effect.
#
# Both anomalies use the same historical reference period
# (2013–2023) and are measured in degrees Celsius.
#
# This allows us to compare the magnitude and timing of
# temperature changes directly on the same graph.
#
# Questions:
# 1. When do soil and air temperature anomalies begin to diverge?
# 2. How much larger are soil temperature anomalies?
# 3. Does soil temperature increase while air temperature
#    remains relatively stable?
# 4. Could canopy removal explain the divergence?
# 5. What other explanations should be investigated?


library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Combine the existing anomaly datasets
# ------------------------------------------------------------

# These datasets were created in the previous chunks.
# No need to recalculate the historical baselines.

robson_temperature_comparison <- robson_soil_anomalies %>%
  select(
    month,
    soil_temperature_anomaly = temperature_anomaly
  ) %>%
  inner_join(
    robson_air_anomalies %>%
      select(
        month,
        air_temperature_anomaly = temperature_anomaly
      ),
    by = "month"
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(
      soil_temperature_anomaly,
      air_temperature_anomaly
    ),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "anomaly"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    variable = recode(
      variable,
      soil_temperature_anomaly = "Soil temperature",
      air_temperature_anomaly = "Air temperature"
    )
  )


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Plot soil and air temperature anomalies together
# ------------------------------------------------------------

ggplot(
  robson_temperature_comparison,
  aes(
    x = month,
    y = anomaly,
    colour = variable
  )
) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed",
    colour = "grey50"
  ) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(
      "Soil temperature" = "firebrick",
      "Air temperature" = "steelblue"
    )
  ) +
  scale_x_date(
    date_breaks = "3 months",
    date_labels = "%b %Y"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Robson Creek: soil versus air temperature anomalies",
    subtitle = "Relative to the 2013–2023 seasonal baseline",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Temperature anomaly (°C)",
    colour = "Variable"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(
      angle = 45,
      hjust = 1
    ),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Interpretation
# ------------------------------------------------------------

# Do soil and air temperature anomalies follow similar
# patterns before 2024?
#
# When does the soil temperature anomaly begin to increase
# more rapidly than the air temperature anomaly?
#
# How large is the difference by late 2025?
#
# Is the divergence consistent with a change in shading
# or soil surface exposure following tree removal?
#
# Could sensor relocation, instrument changes or changes
# in measurement depth explain some of the divergence?
#
# IMPORTANT:
# This graph demonstrates differences in temperature
# anomalies but does not establish the cause.
# Confirm the tree-removal date and sensor history
# before drawing conclusions.

```

```{r}
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Robson Creek: comparison of four environmental anomalies
# ------------------------------------------------------------

# Scientific investigation
#
# Did soil temperatures increase because the surrounding air
# became hotter, or because conditions at the soil surface changed?
#
# If soil temperature rises dramatically while air temperature
# maintains its previous seasonal pattern, that would strengthen
# the case for a local canopy effect.
#
# How do soil temperature, air temperature, soil moisture and
# precipitation anomalies compare over the same period?

# All anomalies are calculated relative to the 2013–2023
# historical seasonal baseline for Robson Creek.

# Temperature anomalies are measured in degrees Celsius.
# Soil moisture anomalies are measured in percentage points.
# Precipitation anomalies are measured in millimetres.
#
# Each variable has its own y-axis scale to avoid misleading
# comparisons between different measurement units.
#

# these months as evidence of drought.


library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

  full_join(

    x = "Month",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(
      angle = 45,
      hjust = 1
    )
  )


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Interpretation
# ------------------------------------------------------------

# 1. When does the soil temperature anomaly begin to diverge
#    from the air temperature anomaly?
#
# 2. Does the increase in soil temperature precede the
#    decline in soil moisture?
#
# 3. Do negative precipitation anomalies coincide with
#    negative soil moisture anomalies?

# 4. Could reduced rainfall explain the soil temperature
#    increase, or did warming begin earlier?

# Consider:

# - Sensor maintenance and calibration records

# IMPORTANT:
# These patterns demonstrate associations and departures
```

```{r}
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Robson Creek: temporal coverage of bird acoustic records
# ------------------------------------------------------------

# Scientific investigation
#
# How long have acoustic records been collected for each species?
#
# Do the records overlap with the environmental changes
# observed at Robson Creek during 2024–2025?
#
# Are there gaps in the monitoring period?

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(lubridate)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Identify the nine Robson Creek species datasets
# ------------------------------------------------------------

species_names <- c(
  "Gerygone_mouki",
  "Macropygia_phasianella",
  "Megaloprepia_magnifica",
  "Meliphaga_lewinii",
  "Orthonyx_spaldingii",
  "Ptilinopus_superbus",
  "Rhipidura_albiscapa",
  "Rhipidura_rufifrons",
  "Sericornis_magnirostra"
)

# Search the existing workshop folder and its subfolders.

species_files <- list.files(
  path = folder,
  pattern = "\\.csv$",
  recursive = TRUE,
  full.names = TRUE
)

species_files <- species_files[
  vapply(
    basename(species_files),
    function(x) any(vapply(
      species_names,
      grepl,
      logical(1),
      x = x,
      fixed = TRUE
    )),
    logical(1)
  )
]

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Extract the dates from each dataset
# ------------------------------------------------------------

species_coverage <- lapply(species_files, function(file) {

  data <- read.csv(file, check.names = FALSE)

  # Identify a date or timestamp column.

  date_columns <- grep(
    "date|timestamp|recorded|eventstart",
    names(data),
    ignore.case = TRUE,
    value = TRUE
  )

  if (length(date_columns) == 0) {
    stop(paste("No date column found in:", basename(file)))
  }

  # Convert the first matching column to dates.

  dates <- as.Date(
    parse_date_time(
      as.character(data[[date_columns[1]]]),
      orders = c(
        "ymd HMS", "ymd HM", "ymd",
        "dmy HMS", "dmy HM", "dmy",
        "mdy HMS", "mdy HM", "mdy"
      ),
      quiet = TRUE
    )
  )

  # Extract the species name from the filename.

  species <- species_names[
    vapply(
      species_names,
      function(x) grepl(x, basename(file), fixed = TRUE),
      logical(1)
    )
  ][1]

  data.frame(
    species = gsub("_", " ", species),
    date = dates
  )

}) %>%
  bind_rows() %>%
  filter(!is.na(date))

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Identify months containing acoustic records
# ------------------------------------------------------------

# Plot actual months with records rather than joining the
# first and last dates across potentially large data gaps.

species_months <- species_coverage %>%
  mutate(month = floor_date(date, "month")) %>%
  distinct(species, month)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Plot temporal coverage for each species
# ------------------------------------------------------------

ggplot(
  species_months,
  aes(x = month, y = species)
) +
  geom_tile(
    fill = "steelblue",
    height = 0.7,
    width = 25
  ) +
  scale_x_date(
    date_breaks = "1 year",
    date_labels = "%Y"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Robson Creek: temporal coverage of bird acoustic records",
    subtitle = "Coloured months contain acoustic records",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Species"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(colour = "black"),
    axis.text.y = element_text(colour = "black"),
    axis.title = element_text(colour = "black"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Questions for interpretation
# ------------------------------------------------------------

# 1. Which species have the longest acoustic records?
#
# 2. Are all nine species monitored over the same period?
#
# 3. Are there gaps in acoustic monitoring?
#
# 4. Do any records extend into 2024–2025?
#
# 5. Which species have sufficient temporal coverage
#    for investigating ecological change?

```

```{r}
# ------------------------------------------------------------

#

# ------------------------------------------------------------

  filter(grepl("Tumbarumba", site_name, ignore.case = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(month = floor_date(as.Date(start_date_time), "month")) %>%
  group_by(month) %>%
  summarise(
    value = if (all(is.na(mean_soil_temp_degC))) NA_real_
            else mean(mean_soil_temp_degC, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(variable = "Soil temperature (°C)")

# ------------------------------------------------------------

            else mean(mean_swc_percent, na.rm = TRUE),

  )
```

```{r}
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Ecoacoustics: species and monitoring site summary
# ------------------------------------------------------------

# Scientific investigation
#
# Which bird species are represented in our acoustic datasets?
# Are any species recorded at more than one monitoring site?
# Which species could support comparisons between sites?

library(dplyr)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Extract species and site information
# ------------------------------------------------------------

acoustic_sites <- bind_rows(
  lapply(names(acoustic_data), function(file) {

    data <- acoustic_data[[file]]

    if (!"SiteName" %in% names(data)) {
      return(NULL)
    }

    species <- sub(".*-", "", sub("-TERNJCU.*", "", file))

    # Extract the scientific name from the filename.
    species <- sub(".*(?:NSW|QLD)-", "", file)
    species <- sub("-TERNJCU.*", "", species)

    data.frame(
      species = gsub("_", " ", species),
      site = data$SiteName
    )
  })
) %>%
  filter(!is.na(site), site != "") %>%
  distinct(species, site)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Summarise all species and their sites
# ------------------------------------------------------------

species_site_summary <- acoustic_sites %>%
  group_by(species) %>%
  summarise(
    number_of_sites = n_distinct(site),
    sites = paste(sort(unique(site)), collapse = ", "),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(number_of_sites), species)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Display results directly in the Console
# ------------------------------------------------------------

cat("\nSPECIES AND MONITORING SITES\n\n")

print(
  species_site_summary,
  n = Inf,
  width = Inf
)

cat(
  "\nSpecies found at multiple sites:",
  sum(species_site_summary$number_of_sites > 1),
  "\n"
)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Questions for interpretation
# ------------------------------------------------------------

# 1. Are any species represented at multiple sites?
# 2. Which species and sites could be compared?
# 3. Should we focus on seasonal activity at one site instead?
```

```{r}

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Grey Fantail: seasonal vocal activity across five sites
# ------------------------------------------------------------

# Scientific investigation
#
# Does Grey Fantail vocal activity exhibit seasonal patterns?
#
# Are seasonal patterns consistent across Australian
# monitoring sites with different environmental conditions?
#
# Vocal activity is measured as the percentage of recorded
# 3-second windows containing at least one vocalisation.
#
# This is an index of acoustic activity, not bird abundance.

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(lubridate)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Combine Grey Fantail datasets
# ------------------------------------------------------------

grey_activity <- bind_rows(
  lapply(grey_fantail_files, function(file) {

    data <- acoustic_data[[file]]

    # Identify the recording date column.

    date_column <- grep(
      "date|timestamp|eventstart|recorded",
      names(data),
      ignore.case = TRUE,
      value = TRUE
    )[1]

    dates <- as.Date(
      parse_date_time(
        as.character(data[[date_column]]),
        orders = c("ymd HMS", "ymd HM", "ymd",
                   "dmy HMS", "dmy HM", "dmy"),
        quiet = TRUE
      )
    )

    data.frame(
      site = data$SiteName,
      date = dates,
      vocal_windows = as.numeric(
        data[["number of 3-sec windows with ≥1 vocalisation"]]
      ),
      total_windows = as.numeric(
        data[["total 3-sec windows recorded that day"]]
      )
    )
  })
) %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(date),
    !is.na(vocal_windows),
    !is.na(total_windows),
    total_windows > 0
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    month = month(date),
    vocal_activity = 100 * vocal_windows / total_windows
  )

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Calculate seasonal vocal activity
# ------------------------------------------------------------

# Sum detections and recording effort within each month.
# This avoids giving low-effort days disproportionate weight.

grey_seasonal <- grey_activity %>%
  group_by(site, month) %>%
  summarise(
    vocal_windows = sum(vocal_windows),
    total_windows = sum(total_windows),
    vocal_activity = 100 * vocal_windows / total_windows,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Plot seasonal patterns across sites
# ------------------------------------------------------------

ggplot(
  grey_seasonal,
  aes(x = month, y = vocal_activity, colour = site, group = site)
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = 1:12,
    labels = month.abb
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Grey Fantail: seasonal vocal activity",
    subtitle = "Proportion of recorded 3-second windows with vocalisations",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Vocal activity (%)",
    colour = "Monitoring site"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(colour = "black"),
    axis.text.y = element_text(colour = "black"),
    axis.title = element_text(colour = "black"),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Questions for interpretation
# ------------------------------------------------------------

# 1. Is Grey Fantail vocal activity seasonal?
#
# 2. Which months show the greatest vocal activity?
#
# 3. Are seasonal peaks consistent across monitoring sites?
#
# 4. Could differences reflect climate, breeding activity
#    or other ecological factors?
#
# 5. Could temperature anomalies and precipitation help
#    explain variation after accounting for season?

```

#check to see what environmental drivers may match vocal patterns of grey fantail

```{r}


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Tumbarumba: environmental data coverage, 2012–2019
# ------------------------------------------------------------

# Scientific investigation
#
# Which environmental measurements are available during
# the Grey Fantail acoustic monitoring period?
#
# Examine air temperature, soil temperature, soil moisture
# and precipitation before selecting explanatory variables.

library(dplyr)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Define the acoustic monitoring period
# ------------------------------------------------------------

tumba_start <- as.Date("2012-09-28")
tumba_end <- as.Date("2019-12-10")

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Function to summarise environmental data coverage
# ------------------------------------------------------------

check_coverage <- function(data, measurement, label) {

  # Identify records for Tumbarumba during the acoustic period.

  site_data <- data %>%
    filter(
      grepl("Tumbarumba", site_name, ignore.case = TRUE),
      as.Date(start_date_time) >= tumba_start,
      as.Date(start_date_time) <= tumba_end,
      !is.na(.data[[measurement]])
    )

  # Return a single summary row, including when no data
  # are available, without producing Inf or -Inf dates.

  data.frame(
    variable = label,
    first_record = if (nrow(site_data) > 0)
      as.character(min(as.Date(site_data$start_date_time)))
    else NA_character_,
    last_record = if (nrow(site_data) > 0)
      as.character(max(as.Date(site_data$start_date_time)))
    else NA_character_,
    observations = nrow(site_data),
    days = n_distinct(as.Date(site_data$start_date_time))
  )
}

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Check all four environmental variables
# ------------------------------------------------------------

tumba_environment_coverage <- bind_rows(

  check_coverage(
    GERI_airtemperature_30min,
    "mean_air_temp_degC",
    "Air temperature"
  ),

  check_coverage(
    GERI_soiltemperature_30min,
    "mean_soil_temp_degC",
    "Soil temperature"
  ),

  check_coverage(
    GERI_soilmoisture_30min,
    "mean_swc_percent",
    "Soil moisture"
  ),

  check_coverage(
    GERI_precipitation_60min,
    "bulk_precipitation_mm",
    "Precipitation"
  )

)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Display the results
# ------------------------------------------------------------

print(tumba_environment_coverage, row.names = FALSE)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Questions for interpretation
# ------------------------------------------------------------

# 1. Which environmental variables overlap with the
#    Grey Fantail acoustic monitoring period?
#
# 2. Are any variables missing or poorly represented?
#
# 3. Which variables could help explain variation in
#    seasonal Grey Fantail vocal activity?
#
# 4. Should temperature anomalies, soil moisture and
#    precipitation be investigated together or separately?


```
